title: Tariffs to Protect Manufacturing
resolution: Resolved: The United States should use broad tariffs to protect domestic manufacturing.
summary: Tariffs are taxes on imports. Supporters see them as a tool to rebuild factories and secure supply chains; critics see higher prices and retaliation. Which is right?

background.p: A **tariff** is a tax on imported goods, paid when the goods enter the country. Tariffs make imports more expensive, which can help domestic producers compete but raises costs for buyers, including American factories that use imported parts. Tariffs are as old as the country. Until the Civil War, customs duties supplied most of the federal government's money, and they stayed its largest single source until the income tax began in 1913. Alexander Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) listed "protecting duties" among the ways to build American industry and make the country "independent on foreign nations, for military and other essential supplies."

Tariffs have also divided the country. The Tariff of 1828, which critics called the "Tariff of Abominations," raised duties to protect Northern manufacturers but raised costs for Southern states that exported cotton and bought imported goods. South Carolina declared the tariffs void in 1832, and the Nullification Crisis ended only with the Compromise Tariff of 1833, which lowered rates over several years. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 raised duties on more than 20,000 imported goods. More than 1,000 economists urged a veto, and trading partners such as Canada answered with tariffs of their own. U.S. trade fell sharply in the years that followed. Most economists see Smoot-Hawley as worsening the Great Depression, not causing it. From 1934 on, the country moved toward trade agreements that lowered tariffs on both sides.

More recent cases give researchers numbers to study. In 2002 the United States placed tariffs of up to 30% on many steel imports for three years; they were lifted in December 2003, after a World Trade Organization ruling against them. The U.S. International Trade Commission estimated that steel producers gained, steel-using industries lost sales, and the net effect on the whole economy was a small loss. Studies of the 2018–2019 tariffs found that their cost passed almost fully into U.S. prices (Amiti, Redding and Weinstein) and that, for manufacturing as a whole, higher input costs and other countries' retaliation outweighed the gains from protection (Flaaen and Pierce, Federal Reserve). Tariffs remain a live question in U.S. trade policy.

disputed.q: Do tariffs bring back manufacturing jobs?
positions: Supporters point to industries such as steel that gained output under protection, and to the growth of American industry behind high tariffs in the 1800s.
Studies of the 2002 steel tariffs and the 2018–2019 tariffs found that gains in protected industries were offset by losses in industries that use their products and in exports hit by retaliation.

disputed.q: Did high tariffs build American industry in the 1800s?
positions: Some historians credit protective tariffs, from Hamilton's plan to the high Civil War-era rates, with giving young American industries room to grow.
Other economic historians argue that a large market, abundant resources, immigration and new technology explain most of that growth, and the country might have grown as fast with lower tariffs.

terms.def: Tariffs another country places on our exports in response.
The network of suppliers that provide parts and materials for a product.
The idea that countries gain by specializing in what they produce at the lowest relative cost and trading.
Government action to build up particular industries.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Tariffs can rebuild American industry, protect national security and strengthen workers' bargaining power.

args.claim: Some industries matter for national security.
args.warrant: A country that can't make its own steel, chips, ships or medicines depends on others in a crisis. Tariffs help keep those industries at home.
args.evidence: Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) on making the country independent for "military and other essential supplies"; Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which allows import limits for national security; reports on supply shortages during the pandemic.
args.response: The negative answers that targeted support for critical industries works better than broad tariffs on everything.

args.warrant: When other governments subsidize their industries or keep our goods out, free trade isn't a level field; tariffs give leverage to change those practices.
args.evidence: U.S. Trade Representative reports on foreign subsidies; the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934, which used tariff levels as bargaining chips to win lower foreign tariffs.
args.response: The negative replies that retaliation hurts American exporters, especially farmers, and other tools (trade cases, alliances) can address unfair practices.

args.claim: Manufacturing supports communities and good jobs.
args.warrant: Factory closures hit some towns hard, and service jobs haven't replaced the wages or stability. Protecting manufacturing protects those communities.
args.evidence: Research on the "China shock" (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) and job losses in manufacturing regions; steel producers' gains in output under the 2002 tariffs, as estimated by the U.S. International Trade Commission.
args.response: The negative answers that automation explains much of the job decline, and tariffs raise costs for manufacturers who use imported parts.

args.warrant: Import taxes bring in money that can reduce other taxes or deficits.
args.evidence: Customs duties supplied most federal revenue until the Civil War and stayed the largest source until 1913; the U.S. International Trade Commission's estimate of about $650 million in added tariff revenue from the 2002 steel tariffs.
args.response: The negative points out that the revenue comes largely from American buyers through higher prices, and the 2002 study found it was offset by lower wages and profits elsewhere.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Broad tariffs raise prices, invite retaliation and cost more jobs than they save.

args.claim: Tariffs raise prices for American families and businesses.
args.warrant: Importers pass much of the tax on to buyers, and domestic competitors can raise their prices too.
args.evidence: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019): the 2018 tariffs passed almost fully into the prices Americans paid for imports; the 1828 tariff's higher costs for Southern buyers.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the price effect is modest and is a fair cost for security and good jobs.

args.warrant: Many American factories use imported parts; making those parts more expensive hurts them, and retaliation closes export markets.
args.evidence: Flaaen and Pierce (Federal Reserve, 2019) on the 2018–2019 tariffs; the U.S. International Trade Commission's finding that steel-using industries lost sales under the 2002 tariffs.
args.response: The affirmative argues that short-term costs give way as supply chains move home, which takes years to show up.

args.warrant: When other countries respond with tariffs on American goods, exporters lose sales; the government has had to send aid to farmers to offset losses.
args.evidence: Canada's and Europe's retaliation against Smoot-Hawley (1930) and the fall in U.S. exports; USDA data on farm exports and trade-aid payments after 2018.
args.response: The affirmative replies that retaliation is temporary and leverage produces better trade deals in the end.

args.claim: Targeted tools work better than broad tariffs.
args.warrant: Subsidies for specific critical industries, trade cases against specific unfair practices, and working with allies protect security without taxing every import.
args.evidence: Analyses of the CHIPS Act and other targeted programs; World Trade Organization dispute cases.
args.response: The affirmative answers that subsidies cost taxpayers directly, while tariffs raise money, and allies don't always cooperate.

strawmen.strawman: Tariff supporters don't understand that tariffs are paid by Americans.
strawmen.why: Many supporters accept some price effects as a cost worth paying for security and jobs.
strawmen.steelman: Tariffs protect industries vital to national security, give leverage against unfair trade, and help rebuild manufacturing communities, which is worth modest price increases.

strawmen.strawman: Free traders don't care about factory workers.
strawmen.why: Opponents argue tariffs cost more manufacturing jobs than they save, and favor targeted help.
strawmen.steelman: Broad tariffs raise prices, invite retaliation and, as studies of 2018–2019 show, can cost more manufacturing jobs than they protect; targeted tools work better.

weak.why: Tariffs are paid by importers when goods enter the country; studies find much of the cost passes to U.S. buyers.
Historians and economists see the Smoot-Hawley tariff as worsening, not causing, the Depression. Overstating it costs credibility.
